study_design_identified: Sequential explanatory mixed-methods study combining an observational quantitative panel/cross-sectional regression analysis of 4,218 PAMSIMAS Phase I villages (2014–2018 functionality data merged with PODES village survey data) with comparative qualitative positive and negative deviance case studies in seven Indonesian villages (FGDs, participant observation, and in-depth stakeholder interviews).
why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly employs a primary sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (Section 1, PDF p. 2; Section 2, PDF pp. 5–9), pairing quantitative non-randomized regression modeling of PAMSIMAS village functionality panel data with primary qualitative fieldwork (focus groups, participant observation, and in-depth interviews) in seven positive and negative deviance villages. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, genuine mixed-methods primary studies combining quantitative and qualitative empirical components are appraised with the MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool), using the Quantitative non-randomized block (3.1–3.5) alongside Qualitative (1.1–1.5) and Mixed Methods integration (5.1–5.5).
overall_rating: High methodological concern in quantitative component; moderate-to-low concern in qualitative and integration components (per MMAT 2018 guidance, overall quality is bounded by the weaker quantitative non-randomized component: 3 No and 2 Can't tell in items 3.1–3.5; 1 Can't tell in qualitative items 1.1–1.5; 1 No in mixed-methods item 5.5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its overarching research questions: under what conditions externally established participatory groups sustain collective rural water management beyond project life, what structural and participatory factors explain subnational variation in 10-year water system functionality, and why positive and negative deviance communities succeed or fail against structural expectations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 Introduction (PDF p. 2); Section 3 Conclusion (PDF p. 15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining longitudinal PAMSIMAS MIS functionality panel data (2014–2018) and PODES village census indicators across thousands of Phase I schemes with week-long multi-stakeholder qualitative fieldwork in seven positive and negative outlier villages directly addresses both the broad determinants and micro-level governance mechanisms of sustainability.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Data and methodology (PDF pp. 5–7); Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 8–9); Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: A comparative positive and negative deviance case study approach is well suited to uncover micro-level socio-political dynamics, leader incentives, and street-level collaboration mechanisms that explain why communities succeed under adverse structural conditions or abandon systems under favorable conditions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Teams of two to four researchers spent one week in each of seven villages conducting participant observation, separate men's and women's beneficiary focus groups representing each hamlet, and in-depth interviews with village heads, hamlet/ward chiefs, provincial-to-village project facilitators, water user group leaders/members, and district officials (Public Works, PMD, Bappeda).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the empirical narratives are internally coherent, the paper provides no account of how interview and FGD data were recorded, transcribed, coded, or systematically analyzed across the seven cases; moreover, Banyumas District is named among the four negative deviance villages (PDF p. 13) without substantive empirical presentation, and the village summary appendix promised in Footnote 18 (PDF p. 9) is missing from the published appendices.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2–2.3 (PDF pp. 8–15); Footnote 18 (PDF p. 9); Appendix B (PDF pp. 23–25)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Key claims regarding village authorities reducing socialization transaction costs, granting operational decision space to water user group chairs, instrumental career/political incentives, and elite water capture or apathy are substantiated with specific case details and direct quotations from residents, water user chairs, village heads, and district officials across six of the seven villages.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear conceptual and empirical alignment linking the deviance case selection criteria, multi-perspective village fieldwork, contrasting positive vs. negative governance pathways, and theoretical synthesis on frontline state-society embeddedness (summarized in Figure 2), notwithstanding omissions in formal coding documentation and researcher reflexivity.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.1: Are the participants representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: While PAMSIMAS MIS nominally covers all constructed schemes, Footnote 10 (PDF p. 6) cites 6,507 Phase I villages (removing ~250 for data mistakes) and Figure 1 implies ~6,524 schemes (3,588 = 55% sustainable), yet Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28) analyzes only N = 4,218 villages (2,439 = 57.8% sustainable). Because over 2,000 Phase I villages disappear from the analytical sample without explanation, representativeness of the regression sample cannot be verified.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 & Footnote 10, Figure 1 (PDF pp. 5–6); Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.2: Are measurements appropriate regarding both the outcome and intervention (or exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Both outcome and exposure measurements exhibit substantial validity weaknesses: (1) functionality ('sufficient' water for >80% of beneficiaries) is a subjective judgment gathered by project facilitators who face incentives to overreport success (Footnotes 8 and 10, PDF pp. 5–6), mitigated only by spot calls to an unspecified sample of facilitators; (2) community participation is measured solely by raw log headcount at inception meetings without normalizing for village population; and (3) water quality is crudely proxied by dug-well vs. non-dug-well technology.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 & Footnotes 8–11 (PDF pp. 5–7); Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.3: Are there complete outcome data?
domain_ratings.justification: Within the reported regression dataset (N = 4,218 in Appendix C), counts are balanced across 2014–2018, but relative to the ~6,507 Phase I villages stated in Footnote 10 (minus ~250 data-error removals = ~6,257), roughly one-third of Phase I villages are absent from the panel regression with no accounting for missing outcome or covariate records.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 Footnote 10 (PDF p. 6); Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.4: Are the confounders accounted for in the design and analysis?
domain_ratings.justification: The multivariable Poisson and logit regressions control only for village revenue per capita, dug-well water source, and contemporaneous tariff level (an endogenous post-treatment mediator reflecting ongoing user willingness to pay rather than a baseline confounder), while omitting village population size (which directly confounds raw attendance headcounts), district/provincial governance fixed effects, poverty rate, and distance/transport cost (summarized in Appendix C but excluded from Table 1/A1/Appendix B models).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1 Table 1 (PDF p. 7); Footnote 21 (PDF p. 13); Appendices A–C (PDF pp. 21–28)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.5: During the study period, is the intervention administered (or exposure occurred) as intended?
domain_ratings.justification: The qualitative deviance findings explicitly demonstrate that PAMSIMAS participatory socialization and community-management protocols were not implemented as intended in many villages: in negative deviance cases, socialization meetings were superficial or bypassed altogether, project funds were usurped leaving half-built infrastructure, or village heads captured and enclosed public hydrants.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors provide a clear methodological rationale (citing positive deviance mixed-methods scholarship) for pairing large-N panel regressions of structural and participatory correlates with in-depth outlier fieldwork to uncover the frontline governance mechanisms linking participation to long-term sustainability.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration occurs both through design (using MIS functionality and PODES pollution/economic data to purposefully sample positive and negative outlier villages, then verifying quantitative indicators during village FGDs) and through explanatory interpretation showing how frontline collaboration conditions the effectiveness of inception participation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2 & Footnote 16 (PDF pp. 8–9); Section 3 & Figure 2 (PDF pp. 15–17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The integrated synthesis persuasively explains why raw participation counts and structural endowments only partially predict 10-year functionality, demonstrating how synergistic vs. competitive/apathetic village head–water user group relations generate self-reinforcing collective action or community exit.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.3 (PDF pp. 9–15); Section 3 Conclusion & Figure 2 (PDF pp. 15–17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: By design, the study investigates empirical divergences from the regression predictions (resource-poor/water-polluted sustainable outliers and wealthier/water-abundant abandoned outliers) and explicitly discusses the geographic Java vs. non-Java rival hypothesis in Footnote 21 (PDF p. 13).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF p. 2); Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 8–9); Footnote 21 (PDF p. 13); Section 3 (PDF pp. 15–16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Because the quantitative non-randomized component has serious weaknesses in sample accounting (~6,507 vs. 4,218 villages), subjective facilitator-reported outcomes, unscaled attendance exposure, conditioning on endogenous post-treatment tariffs, and omitted village/regional confounders—and the qualitative component lacks coding transparency, researcher reflexivity, and a promised village profile appendix—the individual traditions do not fully meet their respective methodological standards.

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious concern / Can't tell: Footnote 10 (PDF p. 6) notes 6,507 PAMSIMAS Phase I villages (with ~250 removed for data mistakes) and Figure 1 implies ~6,524 schemes (3,588 = 55% sustainable), yet the regression tables in Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28) include only N = 4,218 villages (2,439 = 57.8% sustainable), leaving over 2,000 Phase I villages unaccounted for across the 2014–2018 panel without explanation of missingness or attrition.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk: Quantitative Poisson and logit models adjust only for village revenue per capita, a coarse binary dug-well indicator, and contemporaneous tariff collection (itself an endogenous post-inception mediator/outcome of functioning systems), omitting village population size (critical when exposure is raw log headcount of meeting participants), district/island governance fixed effects (e.g., Java vs. outer islands noted in Footnote 21, PDF p. 13), poverty rates, and engineering complexity. Qualitative outlier selection is further confounded by geography, with all 3 positive deviance cases in Java and negative cases reported as outside Java (though Banyumas is in Central Java).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak: Formal PAMSIMAS project rules (inception socialization, community cash/in-kind contributions, KP SPAMS water user group formation, rehabilitation grants, and central-to-village fiscal transfers) are described narratively, and qualitative fieldwork effectively distinguishes de jure participatory procedures from de facto street-level collaboration or elite capture; however, the quantitative exposure reduces institutional participation to a raw headcount of Community Action Planning (CAP) attendees unscaled by village population.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk: In the quantitative component, both the outcome (facilitator-assessed water sufficiency, acknowledged in Footnote 10 as prone to positive overreporting because scheme status reflects on facilitators' own performance) and key predictors (unscaled CAP attendance headcount; binary dug-well proxy for water quality) suffer from measurement error. In the qualitative component, World Bank Water Global Practice staff/affiliates evaluated a World Bank-supported program without discussing researcher reflexivity or formal coding reliability.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak in quantitative component, adequate in qualitative component: Quantitatively, village sustainability (consistently 'fully functional' across 2014–2018 without rehabilitation) rests on quarterly facilitator field visits coding whether 'sufficient' water reaches >80% of beneficiaries based on subjective household interviews without metered flow, microbiological water quality testing, or independent audit (PDF pp. 5–6, Footnotes 8 and 10). Qualitatively, week-long village visits triangulated physical system status, service continuity, and household water use across gender-separated FGDs and multi-stakeholder interviews (PDF p. 9).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is cited; Footnote 18 (PDF p. 9) refers readers to Appendix B for village-level qualitative details (water supply conditions, technology, beneficiary numbers), but the published Appendix B (PDF pp. 23–25) instead contains a Poisson vs. Logit comparison and omits the promised village case table; additionally, one of the four named negative deviance districts (Banyumas) receives virtually no empirical narrative in Section 2.3.2 (PDF pp. 13–15).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate to high risk: Quantitative analysis excludes ~35% of Phase I villages (6,507 vs. 4,218 in Appendix C) without selection criteria or comparison of included vs. excluded villages, and excludes rehabilitated schemes by outcome definition. Qualitative purposive sampling of 3 positive and 4 negative deviance villages is conceptually justified via MIS/PODES data (PDF pp. 8–9), but exact village selection rules among eligible outliers and recruitment procedures within hamlets are not fully detailed, and positive vs. negative cases are geographically segregated (Java vs. outer islands, Footnote 21, PDF p. 13).

overall_narrative_summary: Thapa, Farid, and Prevost (2022) conduct a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of 10-year rural water system sustainability under Indonesia's PAMSIMAS program, combining Poisson and logit regressions on project MIS panel data (2014–2018) merged with PODES village data (N = 4,218 villages in Appendix C) with week-long qualitative fieldwork in seven outlier villages (three positive deviance and four negative deviance cases). Appraised with the MMAT (2018), mixed-methods rationale and integration (items 5.1–5.4) are strong: quantitative regressions motivate purposive outlier selection, and multi-stakeholder qualitative fieldwork (FGDs, participant observation, and key informant interviews) persuasively illuminates how collaborative vs. competitive/apathetic village head–water user group relations shape socialization quality, leadership decision space, and sustained user tariff compliance. However, per MMAT guidance that overall methodological quality cannot exceed the weakest component, overall concern is high (low quality in the quantitative component, criterion 5.5 = No). Specifically, the quantitative non-randomized component suffers from (1) an unexplained sample drop from 6,507 Phase I villages (minus ~250 data errors, PDF p. 6) to 4,218 villages in Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28); (2) facilitator-reported subjective functionality outcomes vulnerable to positive overreporting; (3) operationalizing participation via raw log attendance headcount without adjusting for village population size; (4) controlling for contemporaneous tariff collection (an endogenous post-inception mediator) while omitting district/island fixed effects and other baseline confounders; and (5) non-uniform intervention fidelity. In the qualitative component, data collection and empirical substantiation are strong, but analytic coding procedures, researcher reflexivity (World Bank staff studying a World Bank program), substantive coverage of Banyumas District, and the village summary table promised in Footnote 18 (missing from Appendix B) are omitted.
where_found_summary: Research questions and mixed-methods design overview in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Section 1 (PDF p. 2); quantitative MIS/PODES data, functionality definitions, facilitator bias note, and Poisson regression results in Section 2–2.1 (PDF pp. 5–8) and Appendices A–C (PDF pp. 21–28); qualitative outlier sampling, week-long FGD/interview fieldwork methods, and positive/negative deviance case narratives in Sections 2.2–2.3 (PDF pp. 8–15); integrated synthesis in Section 3 and Figure 2 (PDF pp. 15–17).
